Fit a hierarchical signal detection theory model

Source: R/fit-hsdt.R, R/methods.R
hsdt.Rd

Models paired awareness and influence sensitivities and criteria, their population means and between-subject variation. Frequentist estimation uses lme4::glmer(). Bayesian estimation uses brms and Stan.

Usage

hsdt(
  data,
  estimation = c("frequentist", "bayesian"),
  fix_criteria = c("auto", "none"),
  level = 0.95,
  optimizer = "bobyqa",
  priors = usdt_priors(),
  unequal_variances = FALSE,
  latent = c("correlation", "regression"),
  backend = getOption("brms.backend", "rstan"),
  ...
)

# S3 method for class 'hsdt'
summary(object, ...)

# S3 method for class 'hsdt'
print(x, ...)

Arguments

data

A usdt_data object from usdt_data_tasks() or usdt_data_long().

estimation

Estimation framework: "frequentist" (maximum likelihood via Laplace approximation with lme4) or "bayesian" (Hamiltonian Monte Carlo with Stan, through brms).

fix_criteria

How to handle response criteria. "auto" fixes to zero a dichotomized task's criterion when its mean absolute descriptive subject criterion is below 0.02. "none" estimates all criteria.

level

Confidence level for Wald intervals, or credible level for the posterior intervals of a Bayesian fit (default is 0.95).

optimizer

Primary optimizer passed to lme4::glmerControl(). Alternative optimizers are automatically evaluated if the default fails to converge or produces a singular fit. Frequentist estimation only.

priors

A usdt_priors object from usdt_priors(). Bayesian estimation only.

unequal_variances

Logical. Estimate the standard deviation of the signal distribution of each task instead of fixing it to that of the noise distribution. Bayesian estimation only.

latent

How the Bayesian model writes the relation between the two latent sensitivities, which decides where it places the prior on the location of the influence sensitivity: on its mean, by their latent correlation ("correlation", the default), or on the intercept of the latent regression of the influence on the awareness sensitivity ("regression"). Both keep the priors on the awareness mean, the standard deviations and the correlation. Bayesian estimation only.

backend

Stan interface brms uses for Bayesian estimation: "rstan" (available from CRAN) or "cmdstanr" (installed from the Stan R-universe together with CmdStan). As in brms, the default is the brms.backend option, or "rstan" when it is not set. Bayesian estimation only.

...

For frequentist estimation, additional arguments passed to lme4::glmer(). The model formula, family and data remain managed by the package. For Bayesian estimation, sampling options: chains (default 4), iter (iterations per chain including warmup, default 6000), warmup (default 1000, so each chain keeps 5000 draws), cores (chains run at once, default min(parallel::detectCores() - 2, 4), at least 1), seed, control = list(adapt_delta, max_treedepth) (default 0.95 and 10) and refresh (iterations between progress updates of each chain, default 1% of iter, and 0 hides the progress bar).

object

An hsdt object.

x

An hsdt object.

Value

An object of class hsdt containing:

  • $fit: The underlying fit: a glmerMod object from lme4, or a brmsfit object from brms (see brms::prior_summary() and brms::pp_check()).

  • $tests: Summary table for hypotheses H1, H2, and H3.

  • $design: Summary of the model specification.

  • $diagnostics: Convergence diagnostics.

A frequentist fit also contains $pars, the parameter estimates and their joint covariance. A Bayesian fit also contains $priors. Its posterior draws are those of $fit, where b_dA_Intercept and b_dI_Intercept are the mean \(d'\) of the awareness and influence tasks, sd_subj__dA_Intercept and sd_subj__dI_Intercept their SDs, cor_subj__dA_Intercept__dI_Intercept their correlation, b_cA_Intercept and b_cI_Intercept the mean of an estimated criterion (on the classical scale), and b_sA_Intercept and b_sI_Intercept the signal SDs under unequal variances.

Details

Hypotheses evaluated by default:

  • H1: Mean sensitivity difference between tasks.

  • H2: Latent correlation of sensitivities across participants.

  • H3: Latent regression of influence on awareness sensitivity. Its intercept reflects expected influence performance when awareness sensitivity is zero (\(d'_{\mathrm{Awareness}} = 0\)).

When sample sizes or trial counts are low, variance components can reach singular boundaries. In these cases, the function issues a warning, and parametric bootstrap intervals can be calculated using usdt_boot(), or the model can be fitted with estimation = "bayesian".

Bayesian estimation

The Bayesian model places its priors on the mean, standard deviation and correlation of the two sensitivities and on the criteria. See usdt_priors(). The slope and intercept of the latent regression are derived from them draw by draw. The hypothesis table reports the posterior mean and standard deviation, a central credible interval and a two-sided posterior p-value, \(2 \min\{P(\theta > 0 \mid y), P(\theta < 0 \mid y)\}\). The p-value falls below 1 - level exactly when zero lies outside the credible interval, so with the default level = 0.95 a p-value below .05 means that the 95% credible interval excludes zero.

With latent = "regression", the prior of the influence mean moves to the intercept \(\beta_0\) of the latent regression, and the influence mean follows as \(\mu_I = \beta_0 + \rho \, (\sigma_I / \sigma_A) \, \mu_A\). The intercept tested by H3 then has its specified prior, and the correlation (H2) keeps its own. The difference between the means (H1) has an induced, heavy-tailed prior instead, and because the data fix \(\mu_I\), the intercept prior also informs the posterior of \(\rho\). See usdt_priors() and plot.usdt_priors(). The fit samples the same parameters and reports the same hypotheses either way. Near-zero awareness SDs can produce difficult posterior geometry and divergences. A prior with less weight near zero may help, if substantively justified. Inspect its implications with plot.usdt_priors().

With unequal_variances = TRUE, the noise distribution of each task is \(N(-d/2, 1)\) and the signal distribution \(N(d/2, \sigma_s^2)\), so \(d\) is the distance between their means in units of the noise standard deviation, and H1-H3 compare these \(d\). When \(\sigma_s\) differs between the tasks, \(d\) no longer measures the same discriminability in both: the measure comparable with an equal-variance \(d'\) is \(d_a = d \sqrt{2 / (1 + \sigma_s^2)}\), and the mean \(d_a\) of a task is its mean \(d\) times that factor, which can be computed from the draws of b_dA_Intercept and b_sA_Intercept (and their influence counterparts) in $fit. The correlation (H2) is the same on either scale.

The model is a brms model of the aggregated counts, with one prior per parameter and task. It is compiled the first time it is used with a given set of priors, which needs a C++ toolchain, and stays in a per-user cache directory for later sessions. Inspect the reported divergences, tree-depth warnings, R-hat and effective sample sizes before interpreting results.

See also

usdt_data_tasks(), usdt_priors(), usdt_tests(), usdt_boot(), plot.hsdt()

Examples

# Contextual cuing data from Vadillo et al. (2025)
d <- usdt_data_tasks(
  awareness = vadillo_awareness,
  influence = vadillo_cuing,
  subject_col      = "subj",
  condition_col    = "condition",
  condition_levels = c(signal = "old", noise = "new"),
  response_col     = list(awareness = "judged.old", influence = "rt"),
  response_levels  = list(awareness = c(signal = 1, noise = 0),
                          influence = c(signal = "faster",
                                        noise = "slower")),
  dichotomize      = list(awareness = FALSE, influence = TRUE)
)

m <- hsdt(d)

# Full summary table with SDT parameters and hypothesis tests
summary(m)

# Inspect the model formula (influence criterion omitted by default)
m$design$formula
#> cbind(y, n - y) ~ 0 + c_A + d_A + d_I + (0 + c_A | subj) + (0 + 
#>     d_A + d_I | subj)
#> <environment: 0x55ef37d4b9b8>

# \donttest{
# Bayesian estimation. The first call compiles the model.
mb <- hsdt(d, estimation = "bayesian", seed = 1)
